title: How to Copy a Website in 2026: Easy Steps to Save Time and Money
summary: How to copy a website the right way: browser devtools, HTTrack, wget, WordPress migration plugins, builder duplication, and AI cloners, plus what always breaks.
body_text: Key takeaways: "Copy a website" means four different jobs: saving one page's code, mirroring a static site, migrating a WordPress install, or rebuilding a design. Each needs a different tool. Site copiers only capture what the server returns as HTML. Anything a database or JavaScript generates on the fly does not come with it, and the tools' own documentation says so. For your own site, a migration plugin or a host's clone button beats any crawler, because it moves the database too. Copying the structure and rebuilding it yourself is faster than fighting a broken mirror, and it's the only version that produces a site you can actually maintain. There are a lot of legitimate reasons to copy a website. You're moving hosts and need an identical staging copy. You want an offline archive of a site that's about to disappear. You're studying how a layout works. You bought a template and want to duplicate a page. Or you're migrating a WordPress install and would rather not rebuild 60 pages by hand. The methods for those jobs are genuinely different, and most guides blur them together, which is why people end up running a crawler against a database-driven site and wondering why nothing works. This guide goes method by method: browser developer tools for a single page, HTTrack and wget for static mirrors, WordPress migration plugins for a live install, builder duplication for templates, and AI cloners for design starting points. It also covers what reliably breaks, which matters more than the download step. First, a short word on what's legal Copying your own site, duplicating a template you've licensed, and saving a page for personal offline reading are ordinary technical tasks. Republishing someone else's content or design as your own is a different matter, and it's the part that gets people into trouble. Text, images, and code are protected by copyright the moment they're created. A site's underlying layout ideas generally aren't, which is why "steal the structure, not the pixels" is both the ethical and the practical advice. Two technical checks are worth knowing. A site's `robots.txt` file tells crawlers which paths they may fetch, and it's a real standard: RFC 9309 , published by the IETF in September 2022, defines the format and the Allow and Disallow rules. Automated copying tools ignore robots.txt unless you tell them not to, so check it before pointing a crawler at anything you don't own. On the legal side, the Ninth Circuit's ruling in hiQ Labs v. LinkedIn held that scraping publicly accessible pages likely isn't access "without authorization" under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. That's one statute in one circuit, and it says nothing about copyright or a site's terms of service, so don't read it as blanket permission. Copy your own material freely; for anything else, take the structure and build your own. Match the job to the right tool Picking the wrong method is the single biggest time-waster here. This table maps each job to the tool that actually does it. What you're trying to do Use Gets the database? Cost Grab one page's HTML and CSS Browser developer tools or Save Page As No Free Mirror a static site for offline reading HTTrack, Cyotek WebCopy, wget, SiteSucker No Free Move or duplicate your own WordPress site Migration plugin or host clone tool Yes Free tier, paid for large sites Duplicate a page inside a site builder The builder's own duplicate function N/A Included Turn a design into editable code AI website cloner No Free tier to paid Rebuild a site properly on your own stack A designer or developer N/A Varies Read the third column carefully, because it explains most failed attempts. Only the migration tools move the database, and a modern site is mostly database. Worth saying plainly up front, since we get asked this at Awesomic most weeks: if what you actually want is a site of your own that works like one you admire, none of the copying methods will get you there. They're the right answer for archives and migrations, and the wrong answer for building something. How to copy the HTML code of a website page For a single page, the browser already has everything you need. This is the fastest route when you want to read how something was built or lift a specific component's markup, and it's what most people actually mean when they ask how to copy a website code from a live page. Open the page, right-click the element you care about, and choose Inspect. In the Elements panel, right-click the highlighted node and choose Copy, then Copy outerHTML. Switch to the Styles pane to read the CSS rules applying to that element, including which stylesheet each came from. For the whole page, press Ctrl+S (Cmd+S on macOS) and choose "Webpage, Complete" to save the HTML plus its assets folder. Open the saved file locally to see what survived and what depended on the live server. Step five is the reality check. A "complete" save usually renders roughly right and then falls apart wherever the page expected a live API, a login session, or a font served from a domain that now refuses the request. Those five steps are the whole answer to how to copy a website page, and they cover how to copy a website HTML and CSS in one go, since the save pulls the stylesheets alongside the markup. Reading the CSS without copying it If your goal is understanding rather than duplication, the Computed tab is more useful than the raw stylesheet. It shows the final value the browser actually applied after every rule cascaded, which is the number you'd need to match. Note the spacing scale, the type sizes, and the breakpoints. Those three things carry most of what makes a layout feel considered, and you can apply them to your own markup without copying a single line. How to make a copy of a static website with HTTrack HTTrack is the tool most people land on, and it's still the standard answer for mirroring a site you can reach without logging in. HTTrack's homepage, httrack.com (August 2026). It's free GPL software that has been maintained since 1998. The current stable release is 3.49-2, dated May 2017, with a 3.50 beta dated July 2026, and it ships as WinHTTrack on Windows and WebHTTrack on Linux, Unix and BSD. It downloads a site into a local directory, rebuilds the original relative link structure, and can resume interrupted downloads or update an existing mirror rather than starting over. The setup is a wizard rather than a command line: Install WinHTTrack and create a new project with a name and a destination folder. Paste the target URL and choose "Download web site" as the action. Open Set options, then the Limits tab, and set a maximum mirroring depth of 3 to 5 so you don't pull the entire internet through outbound links. On the Spider tab, decide how to handle robots.txt rules before you start. Under Flow control, lower the connections per second if you're copying a small server, so you don't hammer it. Start the mirror and open `index.html` in the destination folder when it finishes. Depth is the setting people get wrong. Leaving it unlimited on a site with pagination or filters can generate tens of thousands of near-identical pages and run for hours. Cyotek WebCopy and wget, and what they miss Cyotek WebCopy is the other common Windows option, and the Reddit thread below is a good example of it succeeding where HTTrack stalled. Cyotek WebCopy's product page, cyotek.com (August 2026). What makes its documentation genuinely useful is that it states its own limits plainly. WebCopy "does not include a virtual DOM or any form of JavaScript parsing," so if a site uses JavaScript to generate its links, the crawler can't discover the pages it should be fetching. It also "does not download the raw source code of a web site, it can only download what the HTTP server returns," and warns that "advanced data driven websites may not work as expected once they have been copied." That's the honest description of every tool in this category, including HTTrack. On Linux or macOS, wget does the same job in one line: `wget --mirror --convert-links --adjust-extension --page-requisites --no-parent https://example.com` Those flags mirror the site, rewrite links to work locally, add `.html` extensions where needed, pull in the CSS and images each page requires, and stop it from climbing above the starting directory. What always breaks, and why The most useful answer on this topic came from a Reddit thread, not a blog post. In r/hacking , a student trying to preserve a school site full of lecture material got the usual HTTrack and wget recommendations. One commenter added the thing that actually matters: if the site uses a database, a crawler misses those calls entirely, and you end up able to browse only whatever was available as HTML. The original poster eventually succeeded with Cyotek WebCopy after struggling with password-protected areas in HTTrack. That's anecdotal, but it matches what Cyotek's own documentation says, and it predicts almost every failure you'll hit. What you'll lose Why What to do instead Search, filters, comments, logins They query a database that isn't in the copy Migrate the database, or accept a read-only archive Content behind a login The crawler has no session Use the tool's authentication options, if you're authorized JavaScript-rendered pages and links No DOM, no JS execution in the crawler Use a headless-browser crawler, or copy pages individually Contact and signup forms The server-side handler stays behind Rebuild the form against your own backend Fonts and assets on a CDN Requests to other domains often fail or are blocked Self-host the assets you're licensed to use Anything personalized per visitor Generated per session Not recoverable by copying Once you've read that list, the calculation usually changes. For anything beyond a brochure site, mirroring produces a museum piece rather than a working website. How to copy a WordPress website properly WordPress is the case where crawlers are the wrong answer entirely, because the content lives in a MySQL database and the crawler only sees the rendered output. If you want to know how to make a copy of a website you own, this is the section that applies. Use a migration plugin instead. Duplicator, All-in-One WP Migration, and UpdraftPlus all package the database plus `wp-content` into an archive you restore on the destination, and each has a free tier that covers a typical site. Most managed WordPress hosts also have a one-click staging or clone function that does the same thing without a plugin. The sequence is the same whichever you choose. Take a full backup first, generate the package, create an empty destination install, restore, then update the site URLs so internal links and image paths point at the new domain. Skipping that last step is why a migrated site loads with no styling. Two things reliably catch people out. Large sites hit PHP memory and execution-time limits mid-export, which is what the paid tiers mostly solve. And licensed premium themes and plugins usually need reactivating on the new domain, since the license is keyed to a URL. If you'd rather hand this over, our roundup of WordPress design agencies covers who does migrations well. Duplicating pages and templates inside a site builder If you're asking how to copy a website template you already own, the builder almost always has a native duplicate function, and it's the correct tool. Webflow, Framer, Squarespace, Wix and Shopify all let you duplicate a page or a whole site inside your own account, which preserves the CMS structure that an external crawler would flatten. Cloning across accounts is more restricted and depends on each platform's sharing or transfer feature. The thing worth checking before you buy a template is what happens when you change it. A template that looks close to your brand is often harder to adapt than a simpler one, because every custom section fights the original's assumptions. Our comparison of templates versus custom design covers where that trade-off lands. Platform choice shapes how painful duplication is later, which is the practical argument in our Webflow vs WordPress comparison. How to copy a website with AI AI website cloners are the newest category, and they're genuinely useful for one specific job: turning a design you like into editable code as a starting point. Tools like UXPilot's website cloner and Anima's link-to-code feature take a URL or a screenshot and generate HTML, CSS, or React components. What comes out is a visual approximation with a real component structure, which is a much better starting point than an empty file. What they don't give you is a working site. There's no backend, no CMS, no forms that submit anywhere, and the generated code usually needs restructuring before it's maintainable. Treat the output as a fast wireframe with the styling filled in, not as a finished product. The honest use case is speed of exploration. Generating three variants of a layout in ten minutes to see which direction feels right is a good use of the technology. Shipping the output is where it turns into technical debt you didn't write and don't understand. That trade-off shows up across every automated pipeline, and our guide to content creation automation draws the same line: generate to explore, review before anything reaches an audience. Once a page is live, improving it becomes a growth design problem rather than a copying one. How to copy a website and make it your own This is the request underneath most of the others, and the good news is that it's the cheapest path. What you actually want from a site you admire is its decisions, and those transfer without copying anything. Write down what the page does structurally: what appears above the fold, how many sections before the first call to action, what proof it shows and where, how the navigation is grouped, and what it deliberately leaves out. That's a brief, and it's the valuable part. Then rebuild it with your own content and brand. You'll end up with something you can edit, that loads properly, that doesn't carry another company's assumptions, and that nobody can send you a takedown notice about. Our post on easy design hacks covers the specific moves that make the biggest visual difference. That rebuild is most of what our web team does at Awesomic. Clients arrive with three sites they like and a rough sense of why, and the work is turning that into a structure that fits their own content. We run it on a flat monthly fee rather than a per-project quote, so the revisions don't come with a change order. Our web design and WordPress pages cover how that works. Pick the method that matches the job If it's your own site, use a migration tool and move the database. If it's a static site you want offline, HTTrack or wget will do it in an afternoon. If it's a design you admire, write down its structure and build your own version, because that's the only outcome you can actually maintain. The expensive mistake is spending two days fixing a broken mirror and ending up with a site you can't edit. If the goal is a working site rather than an archive, Awesomic matches you with a vetted web designer in up to 24 hours, with unlimited revisions on one monthly fee. Compare the options in our breakdown of monthly web design packages and our list of website design agencies , or Get started directly. FAQ How do I copy an entire website for offline viewing? Use HTTrack on Windows, or wget with the `--mirror --convert-links --page-requisites` flags on macOS and Linux. Set a crawl depth of 3 to 5 so you don't pull in the whole internet through outbound links. You'll get the static HTML, CSS and images, but nothing that depends on a database or a login, so treat the result as a read-only archive. Can I copy a website's HTML and CSS from my browser? Yes. Right-click any element, choose Inspect, then right-click the node and copy its outerHTML, with the applied rules visible in the Styles pane. Saving the page with Ctrl+S and choosing "Webpage, Complete" grabs the markup plus an assets folder. Either way you're getting the rendered front end, not the server code that produced it. How do I copy a WordPress website? Use a migration plugin such as Duplicator, All-in-One WP Migration or UpdraftPlus, or your host's built-in staging or clone tool. These package the MySQL database along with the files, which a site crawler cannot do. After restoring, update the site URLs so internal links and images resolve, and reactivate any premium licenses keyed to the old domain. Is it legal to copy a website? Copying your own site, a template you've licensed, or a page for personal offline use is normal. Republishing someone else's text, images or code as your own infringes copyright. Layout ideas and structural patterns are generally not protected, which is why rebuilding a similar structure with your own content is both safer and more useful than cloning. Can AI copy a website accurately? AI cloners like UXPilot and Anima will convert a URL or screenshot into HTML, CSS or React that looks close to the original, which is useful for prototyping. They don't reproduce backends, databases, CMS content or working forms, and the generated code usually needs restructuring before it's maintainable. Use it as a starting point, not a finished site.

title: Best Lovable Alternatives: 10 AI App Builders Compared for Production Apps in 2026
summary: Choosing an AI app builder for production apps means weighing trade-offs that prototyping tools never force you to confront: data connectivity, governance, code ownership, and long-term maintenance costs. body_text: Choosing an AI app builder for production apps means weighing trade-offs that prototyping tools never force you to confront: data connectivity, governance, code ownership, and long-term maintenance costs. If you've used Lovable and found it excellent for rapid prototyping but limiting for complex apps, backend logic, or native mobile apps, you're not alone. This guide compares the best Lovable alternatives across eight criteria that matter for teams shipping real software - not just demos. The short answer: There is no single best Lovable alternative - the right pick depends on your team profile. Developer-led teams with existing code benefit most from Cursor or GitHub Copilot. Non-technical users building business apps on existing data should evaluate Jet Admin or Bubble. For browser-based full stack generation, Bolt.new offers the closest experience to Lovable with strong code export. And enterprise teams needing governance at scale should look at platforms with built-in compliance controls and audit capabilities. How We Evaluate AI App Builder Alternatives Eight criteria separate production-ready ai app builders from tools that only shine during the initial ui drafting phase. We apply the same framework to every platform in this comparison, whether it's a visual builder, an ai coding tool, or an all in one platform. Here's why each factor matters for technical evaluators and buyers making a platform commitment: Build Speed and Development Velocity Time from natural language prompts to a working app with real functionality is the headline metric. But iteration speed matters just as much - how quickly can you add features, fix bugs, and respond to feedback? We also consider the learning curve for both developers and non technical users, since a tool that's fast for experts but baffling for business users creates bottlenecks. Data Connectivity and Integration Capabilities Production ready apps need to connect to real data: existing databases, third-party APIs, SaaS tools, and structured data sources like Google Sheets. We evaluate native database support, API integration flexibility, real-time data handling, and compatibility with existing enterprise data infrastructure. Extensibility and Customization Control Can you edit code directly? Export it to GitHub? Build custom ui components and reuse them across the same project? Code export and framework flexibility determine whether you're building on a platform or trapped inside one. Vendor lock in is the central risk here. Authentication, Permissions, and Security Built-in user management, role-based access controls, and enterprise authentication integrations (SSO, LDAP, SCIM) are non-negotiable for production apps. We also evaluate data security posture, compliance certifications (SOC 2, ISO 27001, GDPR), and audit capabilities. Deployment and Infrastructure Options Some teams need cloud hosting; others require on-premise or hybrid deployment. We assess hosting flexibility, scalability under production loads, DevOps integration, CI/CD pipeline support, and custom domain configuration. Governance and Enterprise Controls Version control, approval workflows, change management, and team collaboration features separate enterprise-ready platforms from solo-builder tools. Compliance certifications and enterprise security standards factor heavily here. Pricing Model and Total Cost of Ownership Transparent pricing without usage surprises matters more than headline numbers. We evaluate cost scaling with team size and application complexity, free tier generosity, paid plans structure, and long-term value compared to manual coding or hiring developers. Maintenance and Long-term Viability Platform stability, update frequency, backward compatibility, and vendor financial health all affect whether your apps will still run well in two years. Community support and documentation quality round out this criterion. Lovable Alternatives: Side-by-Side Comparison Platform Best For Starting Price Code Export Deployment Key Strength Replit Full-stack dev teams Free tier; paid plans for advanced features Yes (full code) Cloud-hosted Real-time collaboration + cloud IDE Bubble Complex no-code business apps Free tier; paid from ~$32/mo Limited Bubble cloud Mature visual platform with plugins Cursor Developer teams with existing code Free tier; Pro ~$20/mo Full (your repo) Self-managed Deep codebase awareness V0 by Vercel React UI component generation Free tier with limited generations; paid plans Full React export Vercel ecosystem Clean, production ready ui components Windsurf Budget-conscious dev teams Competitive free/paid tiers Full code access Self-managed AI assisted coding at lower cost Jet Admin Business apps on existing data Contact for pricing React code import Cloud, on-premise, hybrid Extensive data integrations + governance GitHub Copilot Universal AI code assistance Free tier; Pro ~$10/mo N/A (your code) N/A (editor plugin) Broadest IDE compatibility Base44 Rapid full-stack prototyping Starter at $20/mo for 100 message credits Limited Built-in hosting All-in-one with minimal config Bolt.new Browser-based full-stack dev Free tier with 1M tokens/month Full (ZIP/GitHub) Built-in hosting Prompt-to-app in minutes Aider Open-source AI development Free (open source) Full (your repo) Self-managed No vendor lock in, model flexibility The main takeaway: alternatives to Lovable spread across a spectrum from visual tools for non technical users (Bubble, Base44) to developer-focused ai tools (Cursor, Aider, GitHub Copilot), with platforms like Bolt.new and Jet Admin occupying productive middle ground for different use cases. Replit: Best for Full-Stack Development Teams Development velocity and real-time collaboration matter most for distributed teams that need to build, test, and deploy without local setup. Replit provides a cloud IDE for building full-stack applications, eliminating the friction of environment configuration entirely. Key strengths: Replit handles complex logic and backend workflows accurately, making it viable for production apps - not just prototypes Replit allows real-time coding and deployment in the cloud, so multiple team members can work on the same project simultaneously Replit offers a generous free tier with paid plans for advanced features like increased compute and private projects AI assistance is built into the editor, supporting ai generation of boilerplate and ai assisted app building workflows Limitations: Pricing at scale can climb quickly as compute and storage needs grow, especially for complex apps with significant traffic The learning curve for teams accustomed to traditional IDE workflows (VS Code, JetBrains) may slow initial adoption Less suited for teams that need on-premise deployment or strict infrastructure control Best for: Small teams and technical founders who want to go from idea to deployed web apps without managing infrastructure. Replit wins when collaboration speed and zero local setup are priorities. Bubble: Best for Complex Business Logic Without Code Bubble remains the most mature visual platform for building complex business apps without writing code. Its drag and drop interface, extensive plugin marketplace, and workflow engine let non technical users build surprisingly sophisticated applications. Key strengths: Visual editor with a mature drag and drop builder handles app logic, conditional workflows, and database operations without manual coding Extensive plugin ecosystem connects to external tools and services, extending functionality well beyond the core platform Proven track record with thousands of production apps running at scale Ready to use templates and reusable components accelerate development for common business app patterns Limitations: Code export is severely limited - Bubble apps are largely locked into the Bubble ecosystem, creating significant vendor lock in Performance can degrade with complex apps handling large data volumes or high concurrent user counts The learning curve is steeper than simpler no code tools because Bubble's power comes with complexity Advanced customization beyond what the visual tools support requires workarounds rather than direct code control Best for: Non-technical teams building internal tools, customer portals, or marketplace apps who accept the trade-off of limited code ownership for visual development speed. Cursor: Best for Developer-Led Teams Wanting AI Assistance For teams with existing codebases who want ai assistance without abandoning their current workflows, Cursor is the strongest option. It's a code editor with agents - not a visual builder - designed for developers who are already writing code and want AI to accelerate, not replace, their process. Key strengths: Cursor excels at maintaining complex codebases with AI assistance, understanding project context across multiple files for accurate suggestions Full code ownership is inherent: you work in your own repository, and generated code lives in your version control system Agent mode handles multi-step tasks (planning, implementing, refactoring) with human oversight, reducing boilerplate while preserving code quality Team rules enforce coding conventions and architectural decisions, supporting governance within development workflows Valued at approximately $9 billion as of mid-2026, indicating strong financial viability and continued investment Limitations: Not built for non technical users - requires coding expertise and familiarity with development environments No built-in ui generation, hosting, or deployment; you manage infrastructure externally through manual setup Less suitable for rapid prototyping of complete applications compared to visual tools like Lovable or Bolt.new Enterprise compliance certifications are less prominently documented compared to platforms built specifically for enterprise deployment Best for: Developer teams wanting to accelerate existing code workflows with ai coding capabilities. Cursor wins when full control over architecture, code visibility, and development process matters more than speed-to-first-prototype. V0 by Vercel: Best for React UI Component Generation Frontend developers who need clean, production-ready React code will find v0 by Vercel uniquely focused on their needs. Rather than generating full stack apps, V0 generates production-ready UI components with minimal adjustments needed. Key strengths: V0 by Vercel generates polished UI components ready for production - the code quality of its React and Tailwind output is consistently high Tight integration with the Vercel ecosystem means deployment is straightforward for teams already using Next.js V0 has a free tier with limited generations and paid plans that scale with usage Generated code is clean, well-structured React that developers can edit code directly and integrate into existing projects Limitations: Frontend-only focus means you need to supply or build backend logic, authentication, and database connections separately Requires technical skills to integrate V0 output into a complete application - it's a component generator, not an app builder Less useful for non technical users who need a complete working app from a single prompt No built-in hosting for complete applications (though Vercel itself handles deployment of Next.js apps) Best for: Frontend developers and design-focused teams who want ai generation of high-quality ui components that slot into existing React applications. V0 wins for UI quality but requires other tools for full stack generation. Windsurf: Best for Budget-Conscious Development Teams Cost considerations matter for small teams and startups that need ai assisted coding without enterprise-tier pricing. Windsurf offers a competitive value proposition with capable AI coding assistance at price points below most alternatives. Key strengths: Competitive pricing makes AI-powered development accessible to budget-constrained teams Full code access and code export mean no vendor lock in - you own everything you build Supports multiple AI models and provides contextual suggestions within your development workflow Lighter-weight than full-platform alternatives, reducing the learning curve for developers Limitations: Smaller feature set compared to more established platforms - fewer built-in integrations and advanced features Less enterprise focus means governance, compliance, and team collaboration features are less mature Community and ecosystem are smaller, which can affect documentation quality and third-party resource availability Not a visual builder - requires development expertise to use effectively Best for: Cost-conscious technical teams and individual developers who want solid ai coding capabilities without paying premium prices. Windsurf wins on value per dollar for teams that don't need enterprise governance. Jet Admin: Best for Business Apps with Existing Data When your data already lives in databases, APIs, spreadsheets, and SaaS tools, the challenge isn't generating a frontend - it's building secure business apps that connect to what you already have. Jet Admin builds secure business apps on existing data, generating the interface and application/backend logic, then deploying the app to users. Key strengths: Connects to existing databases, APIs, spreadsheets, and SaaS tools with extensive integration support - no need to migrate data to a new platform Supports prompt-based app building, importing existing React code, and AI agents that can read data, call tools, and complete multi-step tasks under permissions and audit controls Enterprise-grade security with role-based access controls, audit capabilities, and governance features designed for production deployment Deployment flexibility including cloud, on-premise, and hybrid options - critical for organizations with strict data residency requirements Limitations: Positioned as an app generation platform rather than a pure code generation tool - teams wanting raw generated code may prefer Cursor or Bolt.new Custom pricing means you need to contact sales for enterprise tiers, which adds friction to evaluation Less suited for consumer-facing web apps or marketing sites - strongest for internal tools, admin panels, and business applications Best for: Teams building business apps, internal tools, and admin panels on top of existing data sources. Jet Admin wins when data connectivity, enterprise security, and governance are higher priorities than rapid prototyping of net-new applications. GitHub Copilot: Best for Universal AI Code Assistance GitHub Copilot offers the broadest compatibility of any ai coding tool - it works across virtually every major IDE and programming language, making it the lowest-friction entry point for ai assisted coding. Key strengths: Works inside VS Code, JetBrains, Neovim, and other editors - no need to switch your development environment Proven track record with millions of developers; extensive documentation and community support Cost-efficient: free tier available, Pro plans around $10/month - accessible for individual developers and small teams Accelerates writing code for repetitive tasks, boilerplate, and common patterns across any tech stack Limitations: Code assistance only - GitHub Copilot does not generate complete applications, handle deployment, or manage databases No visual editing, ui generation, or app building capabilities; it's purely a coding accelerator Less contextually aware of full project architecture compared to Cursor's deeper codebase understanding Cannot replace platform tools for teams needing full stack generation or visual builder functionality Best for: Developers who want ai capabilities embedded in their existing workflow without platform lock-in or switching costs. GitHub Copilot wins for universal accessibility but requires other tools for anything beyond writing code. Base44: Best for Rapid Full-Stack Prototyping Base44 appeals to teams that want an all in one platform for rapid prototyping with minimal configuration. Base44 manages database, hosting, and logic internally without external services, reducing setup complexity to near zero. Key strengths: Integrated backend, database, and hosting mean you can go from prompt to deployed app with minimal manual setup Base44's Starter plan costs $20/month for 100 message credits, making it accessible for early-stage projects Built-in logic and data handling reduce the need for external tools during the prototyping phase Good for quick proof-of-concept development when speed matters more than long-term architecture Limitations: Less customization and code export flexibility compared to platforms like Bolt.new or Cursor Newer platform with a smaller community - less documentation, fewer tutorials, fewer third-party integrations Advanced customization beyond what the platform supports may require migrating to a different tool Not ideal for complex apps with sophisticated backend logic or heavy external integration requirements Best for: Teams needing fast proof-of-concept development with minimal configuration. Base44 wins for speed-to-first-prototype when you don't yet need production-grade architecture. Bolt.new: Best for Browser-Based Development Bolt.new is the closest direct alternative to Lovable in terms of workflow: describe what you want in natural language, get a working app, iterate via prompt or code editor. Bolt.new generates full-stack apps from prompts in minutes, with responsive apps built by default. Key strengths: Bolt.new offers a free tier with 1M tokens/month - generous enough for meaningful experimentation Bolt.new generates readable, well-organized React code that you can export as a ZIP or sync via github integration Bolt.new offers one-click deployments and built-in hosting, eliminating deployment friction entirely Browser-based development means zero local setup - access from any machine, instantly Over 5.9 million apps created on the platform, demonstrating significant community adoption Supports integrations with Figma, Stripe, and other external tools for design-to-code and payment workflows Limitations: Scaling complexity: user reports indicate that projects can become unwieldy as dependencies and custom logic grow Mobile apps for app store submission require additional steps outside the platform - native mobile export is limited Enterprise governance features (SSO, compliance certifications, audit controls) are less visible in publicly available documentation Browser-based environment imposes constraints on resource-intensive operations compared to local development Best for: Teams that want the Lovable experience with strong code export and no local setup. Bolt.new wins for browser-based full stack generation but may require supplementing with other tools as complex apps grow. Aider: Best for Open-Source AI Development For technical teams that prioritize transparency, cost control, and freedom from vendor lock in, Aider offers an open-source approach to ai assisted coding. It runs locally, works with your existing code, and lets you choose your AI model. Key strengths: Completely free to use - no paid plans, no credit limits, no token restrictions from the tool itself (you pay only for API access to your chosen AI model) Full code visibility and code control: everything runs in your repository with standard version control Model flexibility: use OpenAI, Anthropic, local models, or any compatible provider No vendor lock in of any kind - if you stop using Aider, your code is unchanged Limitations: Requires significant technical expertise: command-line interface, local setup of development environments, and API key management No visual editing, ui generation, drag and drop building, or hosting - purely a terminal-based coding assistant Self-managed infrastructure means you handle deployment, databases, authentication, and everything else independently Smaller community compared to commercial tools, though active open-source contribution provides steady improvement Best for: Cost-conscious technical teams and individual developers who want maximum control and transparency. Aider wins for open-source ai development but demands the most technical investment of any option on this list. Which Lovable Alternative Should You Choose? Choose Replit if you need cloud-based collaboration and full-stack AI development without managing infrastructure Choose Bubble if you want visual development for complex business applications and accept limited code export Choose Cursor if you have existing codebases and want ai assisted coding with full code ownership Choose Jet Admin if you build business apps connected to existing data sources and need enterprise governance Choose V0 if you focus on React frontends with clean, production ready code and will handle backend separately Choose Windsurf if budget constraints are primary and you have development expertise on the team Choose GitHub Copilot if you want universal AI code assistance across any IDE without switching platforms Choose Base44 if you need the fastest path from idea to deployed prototype with minimal configuration Choose Bolt.new if you want the closest Lovable-like experience with strong code export and browser-based development Choose Aider if you prioritize open-source transparency and want no vendor dependencies The strongest overall recommendation for most teams evaluating alternatives to Lovable depends on your data situation. If your data already lives in existing systems, Jet Admin's integration-first approach avoids the migration pain that prompt-first builders create. If you're building net-new applications and want speed with code ownership, Bolt.new offers the best balance. And if your team is developer-heavy with existing code, Cursor provides the deepest ai assistance without forcing you onto a new platform. Migration and Selection Checklist Before committing to any platform, run through this evaluation: Technical evaluation: Audit your current databases, APIs, authentication providers, and hosting infrastructure Map which integrations are required versus nice-to-have Test whether the platform's code export produces artifacts compatible with your existing CI/CD pipelines Team skills audit: Assess your team's comfort level with writing code versus using visual tools Match platform complexity to actual team capabilities - don't buy a developer tool for a business team Consider onboarding time and the learning curve for each platform Pilot project recommendations: Start with a low-risk internal tool (time tracker, approval workflow, dashboard) rather than a customer-facing product Set a two-week timebox to evaluate build speed, integration difficulty, and deployment friction Test code export early - download or sync the generated code and verify you can run it independently Success metrics: Time to first deployed feature Cost to maintain and bug-fix over 30 days Ability to onboard a new team member to the project Whether you can export and run the application outside the platform Recommendations by Team Type and Use Case For Non-Technical Business Teams Prioritize platforms with visual editing, built-in business features, and minimal learning curve. Bubble offers the most mature visual platform for complex apps. Jet Admin is strongest when you need to build on existing data without manual coding. Base44 provides the simplest path for rapid prototyping. Documentation quality and responsive support matter disproportionately for these teams - evaluate support channels before committing to paid plans. For Developer Teams with Existing Codebases Focus on ai assistance that integrates into your current workflows. Cursor provides the deepest existing code awareness. GitHub Copilot offers the broadest IDE compatibility with the least disruption. Aider gives maximum control for teams comfortable with local setup and terminal-based workflows. Code export capabilities should be a pass/fail gate: if you can't extract and run the code independently, the tool creates risk you shouldn't accept for production ready web apps. For Enterprise Teams with Governance Requirements Prioritize security certifications, audit capabilities, role-based permissions, and deployment flexibility. Lovable itself holds SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001:2022 certifications. Jet Admin supports enterprise security with permissions, audit controls, and flexible deployment including on-premise options. Evaluate vendor stability and financial health - a tool that disappears or pivots dramatically creates migration costs that dwarf any upfront savings. Frequently Asked Questions Can these platforms replace custom development entirely? For straightforward web apps, internal tools, dashboards, and CRUD applications - yes, most of these platforms can deliver production apps without custom development. However, applications with unusual performance requirements, complex real-time systems, or highly specialized backend logic will still benefit from manual coding, at least for critical components. The practical approach is using ai app builders for 80% of the work and custom development for the remaining 20%. How do I migrate from Lovable to another platform? Lovable supports code export via GitHub sync. Export your codebase (React + Vite or TanStack Start, depending on when you created the project), then assess compatibility with your target platform. For Bolt.new or Cursor, the React code should transfer with moderate refactoring. For Jet Admin or Bubble, you're effectively rebuilding the interface on top of your data layer. Expect one to three weeks for a typical migration depending on application complexity. What's the total cost of ownership compared to hiring developers? A mid-level developer costs $80,000–$150,000/year in salary alone, plus benefits, tooling, and management overhead. AI app builder costs range from free tiers to enterprise contracts. For small teams building two to five internal tools, platform costs typically run $200–$2,000/month - a fraction of a single developer hire. The break-even favors platforms until your application complexity requires full-time engineering attention, which usually happens when you have more than 10,000 active users or complex custom integrations. How do I evaluate AI app builder security for enterprise use? Request SOC 2 Type II reports and ISO 27001 certification documentation. Verify SSO and SCIM support for your identity provider. Test role-based access controls with realistic permission scenarios. Review data residency options - where is your application data stored and processed? Check whether the platform offers audit logs that meet your compliance team's requirements. Finally, confirm the vendor's incident response process and SLA commitments. Which platforms offer the best long-term code ownership? Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Aider, and Windsurf offer inherent code ownership because you work in your own repository. Bolt.new and Lovable provide strong code export with full React codebases you can run independently. V0 by Vercel generates clean React components you fully own. Bubble offers the weakest code ownership - applications are largely locked into the platform. For maximum flexibility, choose tools where code export is a core feature, not an afterthought. Can I start with one platform and switch later? Yes, but switching costs vary significantly. Moving between code-export platforms (Lovable → Bolt.new → Cursor) is relatively straightforward because the underlying React code is portable. Moving from a no-code platform like Bubble to a code-based tool typically means rebuilding from scratch. The best strategy: choose a platform with strong code export from day one, even if you don't plan to migrate, so you preserve optionality. Ready to build production business apps on your existing data? title: DuPont Launches DuPont™ AmberChrom™ XT SL Chromatography Resins to Simplify Biopharmaceutical Workflows
summary: DuPont today announced the launch of DuPont™ AmberChrom™ XT20 SL and XT30 SL chromatography resins, expanding its bioprocessing portfolio to help manufacturers streamline purification operations for oligonucleotide and peptide therapeutics.
body_text: WILMINGTON, Del., April 14, 2026 — DuPont (NYSE:DD) today announced the launch of DuPont™ AmberChrom™ XT20 SL and XT30 SL chromatography resins, expanding its bioprocessing portfolio to help manufacturers streamline purification operations for oligonucleotide and peptide therapeutics. Oligonucleotide and peptide therapeutics are a growing class of targeted medicines used to treat a range of diseases—particularly genetics and rare disorders, metabolic conditions (such as diabetes and obesity), and some cancers—by precisely modulating specific biologic pathways. These therapeutics require specialized purification solutions to achieve the purity and consistency needed for clinical and commercial production. As development pipelines expand, manufacturers are increasingly focused on improving efficiency in downstream processing to support consistent quality and scalable production. The newly introduced DuPont™ AmberChrom™ XT20 SL and XT30 SL chromatography resins are slurried versions of the company’s existing DuPont™ AmberChrom™ XT resins and are designed to simplify downstream workflows by eliminating the need for resin hydration prior to column packing. The column packing stage can require significant capital investment, including specialized equipment and additional resources, making preparation steps a key operational challenge for manufacturers. By enabling manufacturers to move directly from delivery to column packing, DuPont™ AmberChrom™ XT SL resins help reduce preparation time, limit the need for additional equipment, and streamline purification processes, while maintaining the high resolution required for complex separations. “As oligonucleotide and peptide therapies continue to gain momentum, manufacturers are under increasing pressure to improve efficiency without compromising performance,” said Shane Kendra, Global Bioprocessing Market Leader for DuPont Water Solutions. “With the introduction of DuPont™ AmberChrom™ XT20 SL and XT30 SL resins, we are helping customers simplify downstream processing by removing time-and capital-intensive preparation steps while maintaining the purity and yield required for bioprocessing applications.” DuPont™ AmberChrom™ XT20 SL chromatography resin is the smallest particle‑size resin in the DuPont™ AmberChrom™ XT resin portfolio and is designed for applications that prioritize high resolution. DuPont™ AmberChrom™ XT30 SL chromatography resin offers a complementary option for optimized separations at higher flow rates, providing flexibility across a range of purification and polishing steps for oligonucleotide and peptide manufacturing. DuPont™ AmberChrom™ XT SL resins complement other slurried resin offerings for the company, including DuPont™ AmberChrom™ CG resins designed for chromatographic and capture applications, and DuPont™ AmberChrom™ TQ1 resin, an anion exchange resin designed for high-throughput purifications of oligonucleotides and peptides. To learn more about DuPont™ AmberChrom™ XT20 SL and XT30 SL chromatography resins and the broader DuPont bioprocessing portfolio, visit https://www.dupont.com/water/industries/life-sciences/bioprocessing.html .

title: I'm a Designer. Last Week I Shipped Dark Mode to Production.
summary: How AI tooling closed the gap between design and code at Multifactor — and what it means to be a design engineer now.
body_text: I'm a Designer. Last Week I Shipped Dark Mode to Production. 2026-07-27 Company Design Agentic JB James Burns Design Engineer No ticket. No handoff doc. No waiting for an engineer to find a free afternoon. I opened the design, described what I wanted, reviewed the diff, and merged it. The whole thing went out before lunch. A year ago that sentence would have made no sense coming from me. I'm a designer — Figma is my native language, not Git. But the gap between “I designed it” and “it's live” has basically closed, and I want to walk through exactly how, because I don't think this is a James thing. I think it's where a lot of product design is heading. Dark mode, live in the Multifactor app. The old loop Here's how a UI change used to go. I'd design it in Figma. Pixel-perfect, every state, every breakpoint. Then I'd write a handoff doc — spacing, tokens, hover states, edge cases — and pass it to a frontend or full-stack engineer. They'd build it when they had bandwidth, which was rarely now . It would come back about 90% right, with the last 10% being exactly the details that make design feel designed: the easing on a transition, the way a card reflows at 380px, the contrast on a disabled state. So I'd file feedback. They'd fix it. We'd review again. The old handoff loop: the design intent and the code lived with two different people, and every round trip across that boundary cost days. Nothing here was anyone's fault. It's just that the person who held the design intent and the person who could change the code were two different people, and every round trip between them cost days. For a product like Multifactor — where the surface is a password manager people live inside, and small UI details directly shape whether the thing feels trustworthy — those days add up fast. Joining Multifactor and the moment the loop collapsed When I joined, I came in as a designer. The shift wasn't a job-title change; it was a tooling change. I started chaining together three things that, together, let me hold the design intent and change the code: Figma MCP — exposes the actual design context (variables, components, layout, tokens) from a Figma file to an AI coding agent. Instead of an engineer eyeballing my spec, the agent reads the design directly. Claude Design — where I iterate on the design itself in a canvas, conversationally, before anything touches the codebase. Claude Code — the agentic coding tool that takes the design context and the change I'm describing and produces an actual pull request against our repo. The toolchain in one shot: Figma open, Claude Code pulling design context through the Figma MCP, and a pull request opening on the other side. The unlock is the MCP connection. The design stops being a picture I describe secondhand and becomes structured context the agent can read — the same variables and components I'm working with in Figma. So “match the design” stops being a game of telephone. The receipts Theory is cheap. Here's what's actually gone to production through this workflow. Dark mode The same screen, light and dark. Dark mode is the canonical “easy for users, miserable for the codebase” feature. It's not one change — it's every surface, every token, every state, audited for contrast and consistency. The old version of me would have specced all of it and handed off weeks of work. Instead I worked through it surface by surface: iterate the theme in design, let Claude Code apply the token changes across components while reading the real design context, then review the diff like I'd review anyone's PR. The parts that needed human judgment — accessibility contrast on edge cases, a couple of components with custom states — I caught in review and corrected in the same loop. The dark mode pull request — reviewed and merged like any other. That's the receipt I care about most: dark mode went out as a single reviewed pull request that touched 55 files — +880 / −339 — the kind of change that used to mean weeks of borrowed engineering time. One concrete number beats a paragraph of adjectives. Responsiveness fixes The Multi agent chat, reflowing cleanly from a wide column down to mobile. Responsiveness bugs are the other classic handoff tax — they're invisible until you're at the exact wrong viewport, and they're tedious to describe in a ticket. Now when I spot one, I fix it where I see it. Take the Multi agent chat: the message list and the composer had to hold up from a narrow desktop column all the way down to a phone. I reproduced each breakpoint, described how it should reflow, verified it, and shipped — no ticket, no waiting. And the steady stream of small stuff A steady stream of small fixes — the kind that used to sit in a backlog forever. The headline features get the attention, but honestly the bigger change is the long tail — the spacing nits, the misaligned icons, the hover states that were never quite right. The stuff that used to sit in a backlog forever because it was never worth interrupting an engineer for. Those now just get fixed. What this did to the engineers (it's not what you'd think) The obvious-but-wrong read is “designers don't need engineers anymore.” That's not what happened, and I'd push back on anyone who frames it that way. What actually happened is that our frontend and full-stack engineers stopped building my UI work and started reviewing it. Their involvement didn't disappear — it moved to the highest-leverage point in the process. They're the final gate: they catch the architectural thing I'd miss, the performance implication, the “this should be a shared component” call. That's a far better use of a senior engineer than translating my Figma file into JSX. Review didn't go away — it moved. A real approval on one of my PRs, merged to main. So the pace on UI/UX changes went up dramatically — not because we removed people, but because we removed the round trips. The design intent and the code change now live with the same person right up until the moment of review, and engineers spend their attention where it's worth the most. What “design engineer” actually means now I used to think the line between design and engineering was about skills — that to cross it I'd need to become a “real” frontend developer. I don't think that anymore. The line was never really about skill; it was about who could act on the design directly . AI tooling moved that line, and it turns out the most valuable place to stand is right on top of it: close enough to the design to know what's right, close enough to the code to make it so. I'm still a designer. I just don't hand the design to someone else to make it real anymore. Still a designer — just no longer handing the design to someone else to make real. — James We're redefining zero-trust — so you can protect your accounts with confidence. Multifactor's provably secure zero-trust solutions cryptographically guarantee that only authorized users can access sensitive data, turning identity into your greatest asset in the fight against cyber threats.
